options.text: A platform fork requires a signed contributor licence agreement before it may be created, while a governance fork does not require one.
options.why: Neither meaning of "fork" depends on a CLA; a CLA concerns contributing changes back, not the act of copying a repository.

options.text: A governance fork can only occur with the original project's explicit written permission, since the licence does not grant the right to fork automatically.
options.why: Open source licences grant the right to make and distribute derived works automatically; no separate permission from the original project is required.

items.rationale: In the governance sense, forking is a deliberate, permanent split with independent maintainers; in day-to-day platform vocabulary, "fork" also names a server-side repository copy created as the first step of an ordinary contribution — the opposite outcome.

verification.reasoning: Citation defect fixed before verdict: the item cited osi-osd alone, which defines ten licensing criteria and says nothing about forks, clones or pull requests -- it could not support the key or o2. GitHub's forks documentation states 'Forks are repositories that start as copies of another repository, called the upstream repository. A fork has its own settings and permissions but stays connected to the upstream repository', and its pull request docs describe the fork and pull model in which the fork exists to open a pull request upstream; that is the key's platform fork. The governance fork, a lasting divergence with its own maintainers, is the contrasting sense, and the key states the contrast correctly. o2's why is now verified: git-clone's manual page opens 'Clones a repository into a newly created directory', a local operation, whereas a GitHub fork is a separate server-side repository -- so fork and clone are not the same operation. o3's why is true: nothing in either sense of fork turns on a CLA. o4's why is true and rests on OSD 3, retained in the citations for exactly that claim. Only the key is defensible.

items.stem: What does a neutral foundation such as the Linux Foundation or the Apache Software Foundation actually provide to a project it hosts?

options.text: Legal entity status, stewardship of assets and trademarks, shared infrastructure, and governance rules — not technical direction, which stays with the project's own maintainers.
options.why: A foundation provides legal shelter and governance structure so no single vendor controls a project, without dictating what the project builds.

options.text: Paid engineering staff, employed by the foundation itself, who write and maintain the code of each project it hosts.
options.why: Foundations do not staff their projects' development: the ASF states that all participants in its projects are volunteers and that nobody is paid by the foundation to do their job.

options.text: A guarantee that every contributor automatically becomes a committer with write access after their first merged change is accepted.
options.why: Committer status is earned on merit within each project over time; a foundation does not grant it automatically after one contribution.

options.text: Direct control over each hosted project's technical roadmap, exercised through decisions made by the foundation's board.
options.why: A foundation holds assets and sets governance rules; the technical roadmap remains a decision for the project's own maintainers, not the board.

items.rationale: Neutral non-profits such as the Linux Foundation and Apache Software Foundation hold a project's assets, trademarks, and infrastructure so no single vendor controls it, while deliberately leaving technical direction to the project's own maintainers.

verification.reasoning: REFUTED on o2, then rewritten. The original o2 offered 'a single organisation-wide contributor licence agreement that automatically supersedes each individual hosted project's own agreement', with a why asserting 'CLA terms are set per project even when a shared foundation hosts several of them'. That is false for one of the two foundations the stem names: the ASF's Contributor Agreements page states 'An individual must have submitted a signed ICLA to the ASF before we give them commit rights to any ASF project' -- one foundation-wide individual CLA, not per-project terms. Rather than leave a distractor whose why states a falsehood, replaced it with a paid-staff option refuted verbatim by How the ASF works: 'All participants in ASF projects are volunteers and nobody (not even members or officers) is paid directly by the foundation to do their job.' The key is confirmed by the same page: the ASF was formed to supply 'hardware, communication, and business infrastructure', to 'create an independent legal entity', to shelter volunteers from legal suits and to 'protect the Apache brand'; the board handles 'management of the corporate assets (funds, intellectual property, trademarks, and support equipment)'; and, decisively, 'However, each Apache project's PMC has technical decision-making authority regarding the content and direction of the project.' The Linux Foundation's About page corroborates the neutral-home framing ('a neutral, trusted hub for developers to code, manage, and scale open technology projects'). o4 is refuted by that same PMC sentence. o3's why is true: committership is earned on merit over time. Rewrite added no em dash. Re-verified after the fix.
